A BAD NIGGER,

Whose Neck Should Broken as Soon as He is Caught.

LITTLE ROCK, August 9.—The police have been busy since Saturday working up a case, but so far without success. On Saturday, a negro, a stranger in the city, went to a residence near the corner of Scott and Sixteenth streets and took prisoner a bright mulatto girl. He claimed to be a deputy-sheriff, and served a paper on the girl, who is only about fifteen years of age, and commanded her to go with him to the court. Knowing no better she put on her hat and started. The pretending officer took her into the woods just south of the city, drew a revolver on her, and under penalty of immediate death compelled her to accede to his hellish desires. His purpose accomplished, he left his victim more dead than alive lying in the woods. Some hours after she made her way back to the house, still at the point of death, suffering intense agony. She gave a minute description of the scoundrel, and although seen by several parties no one knows his name or residence.

FORT SMITH, ARK.

An Indian Convicted of Murdering a White Man.

FORT SMITH, August 9.—Sawquaree, a full-blood Sac and Fox Indian, was committed in the United States Court to-day for the murder of an unknown white man in that country in 1879. The jury were out only an hour. It appeared from the evidence that the white man had been employed by Sawquaree to make some rails for him, and while en route to the latter place was attacked by him, shot, and afterward scalped. The scalp was presented about a month later by the noble red man to his nephew, to whom he told the details of the crime. All the witnesses against him were members of his own tribe.

'INDIAN KILLED BY A DEPUTY MARSHAL.

The annexed telegram was received here to-day:

"POWHESKA, L. T., August 9, 1881.

"To V. Dell, United States Marshal:

"I have been in pursuit of Little Buck for five days, and run on him to-day. He, with five others showed fight, resulting in the killing of Little Buck. The Indians are reported in gangs, waiting for me to pull out. I am compelled to wait a day or two for the excitement to subside.

"L. W. MARKS, Deputy Marshal."

Little Buck is one of the chiefs of the Osage tribe of Indians, which, although one of the wealthiest tribes in the Territory, is the most lawless. At the last term of court here six Osages were convicted of horse-stealing, and sentenced to imprisonment at Detroit. Deputy Marshal Marks and his posse, while on their way to this place, were besieged by a band of about 100 Indians, who demanded their release. After much parlying he was allowed to proceed, on a promise that he would not again invade the Territory. It is feared here that he will experience much difficulty in getting out of the country in safety.

Death of our Oldest Citizen.

How It Is Done in North Carolina—Two Ravishers Taken from a Jail by Masked Men and Left Dangling from a Tree.

Hton Point, N. C., June 22.—The details of the lynching of two negroes at Danbury, Stokes County, have just reached here. The place where this affair occurred is about fifty miles from the nearest telegraph-station. John Lindsay and Estes Hairston had been confined in jail for the past seven months for outraging the person of a white girl about 12 years old. Jonkins Lindsay was in jail on a similar charge, in which a white married woman named Gardiner was the victim. Ever since the lynching of the negro in Rockingham County last Saturday week for outraging a prominent lady of that county, Lindsay and Hairston had been very much concerned for their own safety, and several times expressed fears that they would be lynched.

During Monday night a band of 150 mounted and masked men rode into Danbury. A consultation was held, on the outskirts of the village, as to the best and quickest mode to be adopted to obtain possession of the prisoners. In accordance with an agreement, the party drew up to the jail and demanded of the jailers the surrender of Lindsay and Hairston. This was refused; the jail doors were forced open, and the crowd of masked men sprang through the doorway, forced open the doors to the cells of the two negroes, so eared them in a vehicle, and drove them rapidly out of town. As soon as a convoyont spot was found the party halted, formed into a square, and gave the prisoners a few moments in which to prepare for the sudden and horrible death that awaited them. After these preparations the two negroes were placed in a wagon, which was driven under a large oak tree. Matters were placed about the negroes' nooks; the ends of which were thrown over a branch of a tree, and the wagon then driven from under the men, and the two negroes were left hanging. Their bottles were discovered a few hours later where they were left. The names of those who participated in the lynching are not known. The punishment meted out to Lindsay and Hairston is generally approved by both the white and colored people in the community.

C., June 24.—The lynching of the two men a few days since in Stokes County for rape, and the lynching of another one two weeks ago, does not seem to have had the effect looked for by the lynchers. Once he was convicted of an attempt at rape and sentenced to nine years in the Penitentiary, but his counsel succeeded in having his sentence shortened. Officers in Search of an Assassin- The Wrong Man Killed-Corone:'s Inquest- Two Verdicts.
Yesterday morning early there was considerable interest aroused over the report that a colored man had been killed in a row at a dance on the previous night, and that his assailant had subsequently been shot by a policeman, and had died about eight o'clock in the morning at the police barracks, whither he had been removed. Upon investigating this reported double tragedy we learned the following particulars:

On Wednesday night a difficulty occurred at a house near Eastern Hall, in the vicinity of the yard of the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, between two negroes, Elias Harris and John Lanier, which terminated in the latter shooting Harris, who fell to the ground, seriously wounded. Lanier then fled, and a physician was at once summoned to the relief of Harris. Dr. Bulloch responded, and upon examination pronounced the wound mortal. Immediately after the occurrence, Jackson Davis, colored, who was present at the time, proceeded to the police barracks and notified the officer on duty, at the same time stating that he could direct an officer to where he believed Lanier had taken refuge, the shooting having previously been reported by Sergeant Green.

Lieut. Howard, who was on duty, detailed Policemen John Crowley and W. F. Nungazer to accompany Davis, and the party left the barracks shortly after ten o'clock and were pillowed by their guide to the junction of the White Bluff road and the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, about one mile and a half from the city, where are located the quarters for the station hands of the road. On reaching this point the party knocked at the door of the house occupied by Mr. F. M. Murray, the section master, and inquired if there were any strange negroes in his camp. He arose, stating that he did not know, but would accompany the officers and Davis to one of the shanties, on reaching which admittance was demanded. No attention was paid to the demand for some minutes, when the door was opened by a colored man, who looked out, and perceiving the officers, immediately closed the door again and attempted to spring from the window. Finding his escape cut off from this quarter, he swung open the door, and springing outside broke into a run. Davis immediately called out "that's the man," and the officers yelled to the fugitive to stop, but he continued running, when he was fired upon several times. He fell but quickly arose and started to run again, when another shot was fired and he tumbled over on the ground. The party then approached the prostrate man, when it was discovered that he was not John Lanier but a colored man named Isaac Hicks, not the one they were after.

Hicks was found to be badly wounded, having been shot in three places, and was placed in a wagon and conveyed to the police barracks, where he received attention from Dr. J. T. McFarland, who at once pronounced him fatally wounded. He died yesterday morning early. Death at the Infirmary of Ellias Harris. Colored-Coroner's Inquest and Two Verdicts.
Mention has been made in the MORNING News of the shooting of Elias Harris, colored, on Wednesday night by John Lanier, colored, who escaped, and whose pursuit resulted in the killing of an innocent man, Isaac Hicks. Yesterday Harris, who was conveved to the Georgia Infirmary, died from the effects of his wound, which was inflicted in the windpipe. The details of the killing are briefly these:

On Wednesday night, 27th instant, John Lanier entered the house of his husband Martin and asked for some oil, and was told by Martin he had none. He then walked across the room and stood up by the fire. Martin was engaged in writing in an account book and paid no further attention to him. Presently Aleck Martin entered the room from the back door, and was followed by Elias Harris, who went to the fire to get a light for his pipe. A few minutes after the report of a pistol was heard and Harris fell to the ground. Lanier said, "Let me get out of here," and started to run out of the door, and in doing so jumped over the body of Harris. Martin grabbed Lanier and said, "You cannot go out of here," and his brother Aleck also caught hold of him. Lanier struggled to get away, and presented his pistol in the face of Aleck Martin, when Hiram called to him not to shoot. Lanier then managed to free himself and escaped. Hiram Martin stated that the shooting was done without any provocation whatever. He did not see Lanier fire the shot, but he saw a pistol sticking in his pocket when he came into the house.

There were in the house at the time Hiram Martin and his wife, Aleck Martin, Charley Cheeseborough, Anthony Crieg and Ellen Johnson, but none of them saw the sh t fired. There had been, to the knowledge of these parties, no previous difficulty between Harris and Lanier, and there was no quarrel on the night of the shooting.

LABOR RIOT IN NEW ORLEANS.
A Colored Man Shot by a Policeman and the Governor Called Upon for Troops.

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 10.—The labor war culminated in bloodshed this morning, when James Hawkins (colored), a member of the Cotton Teamsters' Association, was shot and instantly killed by Police Sergeant Reynolds. The cause which led to the shooting was the attempted arrest of Hawkins, when a general flight ensued, during which Reynolds's clothing was torn off and missiles were thrown at his head by colored women. As the prisoner was about to escape Reynolds fired two shots. One struck Hawkins in the thigh, passed through, and hit a white man named Pat Connelly in the leg. The second shot struck Hawkins in the forehead, and he fell dead. Intense excitement was created, and matters assumed a serious aspect. Fire alarm bells were rung, which summoned the police force. Several arrests were made for interfering with teamsters. A float of cotton which had been left by the drivers was set on fire. The Mayor has ordered the Chief of Police to close all places where liquor is sold in the vicinity of the troubles, and to arrest any parties failing to comply with the order. The Mayor has forwarded the following communication to the Executive:

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 10, 1881.

To his Excellency Louis A. Wilts, Governor of Louisiana.

SIR: The police force which I have under my control has been overpowered. I have serious apprehensions of further troubles, and do not feel that the police force alone can preserve the peace of the city. I therefore respectfully call upon your Excellency for assistance, that the preservation of the peace may be secured.

Your obedient servant, Jos. A. Snakspzare, Mayor.

The Governor issued orders to Major-Gen. Bahan to have militia regiments ordered to their armories. They were disbanded, however, early in the afternoon, there being no immediate need of their interference. It is understood, however, that they will be ready at a moment's notice.

There was no more trouble after the killing of Hawkins, with the exception that some teamsters returning from the Commercial Press were stoned and hooted at the corner of Orange and Chippawa streets, at 4 P. M. When Officer Brehter ordered the mob to stop he was hit with a stone, and he fired twice without effect.

Collision Between the Striking Laborers and Police in New Orleans—A Negro Killed—Trouble Feared Monday.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

NEW ORLEANS, La., Sept. 10.—The difficulty which evil-disposed persons have for the past ten days tried to bring about culminated in the killing by a policeman of a negro striker who refused to submit to arrest. This caused great excitement, and negro men and women thronged the levee and adjacent streets. Capt. Minor, Chief of the Labor Bureau of the cotton factors, was shot and stoned by negro women. Considerable of a panic followed, and the general alarm was sounded calling out the full police force. The negroes were massed in one quarter of the town, and, having no leadership, nothing was done with them. At noon the Mayor, under influence of some panic, called on the Governor for troops, alleging the police were overpowered. The Governor ordered Maj.-Gen. Behan to respond to the Mayor's request with such full force as was necessary, but on consultation discovered that the militia mainly sympathized with the strikers, and they were not called out. Mean-time the excited crowd dispersed, no other trouble being reported than the occasional brickbating of a non-unionist teamster by irresponsible men and boys. It was thought during the day that an adjustment was being reached, but the action of the authorities during the day seems to have embittered the strikers, and negotiations were declared off. A massmeeting of all the strikers was held tonight, when it was determined to give the dead negro a heroic burial—white and black cooperating. More trouble is threatened on Monday.

THE COTTON STRIKE.
The strike of the New Orleans cotton laborers assumed a very serious aspect on Saturday and Monday last. Strikers congregated on the streets in crowds and assaulted the drivers of cotton floats with stones and clubs, and several serious affrays grew out of the attempts of the police to quell these disturbances. Fortunately only one life was sacrificed—that of a colored man named James Hawkins, who was shot and instantly killed by Sergeant Reynolds of the police while resisting arrest. Finding his means for preserving the peace and protecting the commerce of the city inadequate, Mayor Shakespeare called upon Acting Governor McEnery for aid and the militia was ordered to assemble. Although the occasion seemed to justify the active employment of the State troops to maintain the supremacy of law and order, they were kept cooped up in their armories and rendered no service whatever. Mayor Shakespeare has sharply criticised the inaction of Gen. Behan in the premises and we are inclined to regard his strictures pertinent and deserved. Tuesday night after a long conference of committees representing the Employers Association and the several labor organizations, a basis of compromise was agreed upon which brought the strike to an end. Some modifications in the tariff of charges for handling cotton were made, and the employers carried the point for which they have so strenuously contended from the first, viz: the right to employ and discharge hands free from the interference or dictation of labor unions.

WHAT THE FARMERS HAVE DONE FOR THEIR MICHIGAN BRETHREN.
THERE MICHIGAN BRETHREN.

There seems to be a persistent effort in certain quarters to hold Chicago up to the country as an ungrateful city because her contributions in aid of the farmers who suffered last August by fire in Michigan have not equated the demands or the expectations of some of the persons engaged in making collections for that purpose, although she has already refunded more to Michigan to relieve her burnt-out farmers than she received from all that State ten years ago when ten to twenty times as many of her people were in sore distress. It has pleased these people to remind Chicago that when this city was swept by fire there was no hesitation anywhere in the contribution to the relief of her stricken multitudes.

There evidently is a mistake somewhere on this subject. When Chicago was swept by fire on the eve of winter in 1871 the number of people rendered desolate and homeless was a huge one, and the benovidence of mankind was extended to them, and for this Chicago has always been grateful. The net losses in Chicago were immense—$160,000,000. The contributions of the world, however, were never disparaged because in the aggregate they did not equal 3 per cent of the losses.

The destruction of property in the Saginaw farm districts was a grievous loss to the farmers of three counties. Some hundreds of them were left destitute of even food and clothing, without homes or habitations, losing their season's crop of 1881, and thus deprived of obtaining more except by loans on their land or by charity until the next harvest. They lost all they had except the land, which was swept of its entire vegetation. The number of victims is variously estimated at 1,100 to 3,000 families, and they were all in purely agricultural districts.

These sufferers were almost all farmers, cultivating their farms. In the State of Michigan there were 125,000 other freehold farmers, all of them well to do, and able promptly to assist their suffering brethren in the Saginaw district. In the adjoining States of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, and Wisconsin, there are between one and two millions of prosperous farmers owning rich productive lands, and every one of them naturally and personally interested in the sufferings of the few hundreds of Michigan farmers who with their families had been so suddenly overtaken by this fire calamity. Now, what are the facts? The money raised in Michigan for these suffering farmers has been collected mainly in Detroit and in the other cities and towns of the State. The 125,000 prosperous farmers have practically done nothing to relieve and succor those unfortunate farmers of the Saginaw district. In Ohio, Indiana, New York, Massachusetts, Illinois, and Wisconsin, and all other parts of the country, the contributions in aid of these Michigan farmers have been made in the cities and towns, and scarcely a dollar has been forwarded or given by the agricultural brethren of the West or elsewhere to the sufferers. As a whole, the farmers of these Western States are the most wealthy and prosperous, as they are the most numerous, of the population, and yet they have left the Governor of Michigan and the other gentlemen who have been soliciting donations to importune the cities and towns of the country for aid. Notwithstanding the sufferers were almost exclusively farmers, the farmers of Michigan and all other surrounding States have done substantially nothing in the way of making good the losses of the suffering agricultural class.

The population of Chicago at the time of the fire was, and at this time is, largely made up of laborers and other workmen dependent upon their daily wages. A majority of them do not own the houses in which they live. They are, as compared with the farmers of the Western States, poor in this world's goods. The entire Chicago population lost by the fire; the rich and prosperous were left penniless, and their recovery from these losses has been exceptional. These destroyed capitalists have been succeeded by newcomers, who have brought capital here. Thousands of families once in good circumstances, who lost their entire property in the fire, still suffer under the poverty then entailed, and it is a mistake to suppose, as many of these official people in Michigan assume, that the losses of the Chicago fire were made good by the world's contributions. Four and a half millions of donations went but a small way towards making good 160 millions of loss over and above insurance recovered. But that charity saved tens of thousands of laboring poor from perishing of cold and hunger. It kept them alive until they could find work and become self-supporting.

A letter from Mr. John Forsythe, printed in our last issue, throws some light upon the eagerness of the tenants in the North of Ireland to get court leases, and upon their satisfaction with the new condition of things. Mr. Forsythe refers to the sale of a farm of nineteen acres recently made in the County Autrum, in the North of Ireland, in the neighborhood he came from, which is by no means one of the best of Irish agricultural districts.

The tenant-rights in the little farm of nineteen acres, which had been paying a yearly rental of $160, or two pounds an acre ($10), was put up to auction under the provisions of Gladstone's recent Land act which Parnell despires, and was sold for $3,500, or $194.40 per acre, which represents the tenant's good-will, improvements, and interest in the farm. The inquest was held at the late residence of the deceased at Park Ridge, a plain and unpretending farm-house about a mile distant from the station. Here were gathered a large concourse of people, upon whose minds the sudden taking-off of their aged friends had evidently produced a very profound impression.

As soon as the place was reached, the party were shown into the barn, where the deceased still lay at rest in the wagon in which they had met their death. The evidences of its terrible nature were evident, especially in the case of the old lady, whose body was found to be terribly scarred by the electric fluid and by the flames of her burning clothing, the lightning having set fire to the upper part of her dress. The body was clad very neatly, a black woolen shawl being thrown around a light-colored stuff dress. About three inches below the right arm pit the shawl was slightly singed, a small round hole about the size of a dime having been burned away. Hence this the dress, also burned, but to a larger extent, was found to be torn open while the underclothes below, which at this point had been almost entirely consumed, gave evidences also of having been rent by the stroke. The back and shoulders, and, in fact the whole of the right side of the body, were

SEAMED BY THE ELECTRIC CURRENT, which, instead of penetrating the body, as is sometimes the case in like casualties, had evidently spread and run in divided streams along the flesh. This peculiarly-marked discoloration, which evidenced the passage of the subtle messenger of death, was quite different from that which had been caused by the burning which followed the lightning stroke. The flames of the ignited clothing had soared the left side from the neck down, leaving it in parts a light, and in parts a deep, brown. Notwithstanding the terrible nature of the agency which had accomplished the old lady's death, the expression of her face was perfectly calm and peaceful; in fact, a pleasant smile played around her mouth, while not a suspicion of distortion marred the serene repose of the other features.

NEAL ESCAPES THE HALTER
THE WORK OF A JURY CHOSEN FOR A PURPOSE.
A Verdict that Receives Not the Slightest Popular Sympathy or Approval - How it was Arrived at.
The trial being over and the prisoner acquitted, it is now in order to give the details and the popular opinions of this remarkable case. Neal was first tried at the May term, 1880, after a motion by Mr. Higgins, his counsel, to quash the jury panels by reason of the exclusion therefrom of men of African descent by reason of their race or color, and to remove the case to the United States District Court had been refused. He was then tried by a jury composed of the following gentlemen:

Thos. S. Dixon, Brandywine Hd.
John W. Worrell, Mill Creek.
John Williams, St. Georges.
Hyland P. Bullen, White C. Creek.
Jesse Reeves, New Castle.
Wm. Lawton, Wilmington.
James Vanarsdalen, New Castle.
Aaron H. Paxson, Pencader.
John Thompson, Mill Creek.
Richard Booth, Wilmington.
Deweese Chandler, Christiana.
Joseph H. King, Brandywine.

This jury after an hour's deliberation returned a verdict of guilty on the afternoon of May 26th, 1880, and the following day Nesl was sentenced to be hanged.

The subsequent proceedings, which resulted in a reversal of this judgment and Neal's arraignment for a second trial are well known.

On Friday last Neal's second trial was commenced, and in the drawing of the jury Mr. Higgins was careful to challenge every Democrat and every man on the jury who lived south of the canal. With the exception of the foreman, the entire jury was drawn from Christiana, Brandywine and Wilmington Hundreds, eight of them being from this city. The regular panel was exhausted, and Sheriff Clark summoned talesmen from a previously prepared list, among his names being some men who, if they lived a thousand years in Wilmington, would never be deemed worthy of having their names placed in the box to be drawn upon the regular panel. His proceedings in drawing talesmen for the Harrigan jury were in marked contrast, as on this occasion he called upon reputable and well-known citizens of New Castle county. Finally this remarkable jury, evidently chosen for a deliberate purpose, was selected, as follows:

DAVID R. CHOATE, White Clay Creek Hd.
WM. B. ADAMS, Wilmington.
NEHEMIAH DAVIS, New Castle.
WM. MURPHY, Wilmington.
WM. B. BANCROFT, Christiana.
MATTHEW MACKLEM, Wilmington.
PETER WOOD, Wilmington.
JOHN NICHOLS, Wilmington.
SAMUEL G, LOGAN, Wilmington.
CHARLES H. HOWARD, Wilmington.
GEO. D. WATSON, Wilmington.
ALBERT I. DERRICKSON, Brandywine.
It was a representative jury in one respect, at least. It represented Republican sentiment generally and the Republican party of New Castle county most admirably.
The jury drawn the trial proceeded. The State made a plain case. The evidence of the prosecuting witness was not impeached in the slightest particular, and the defense made practically no defense whatever. Mr. Higgins gave the jury the key note in his closing argument, when he brutally said he would treat the evidence of the prosecuting witness,—the poor, outraged white woman—as a lie, for such he believed it to be. Judge Houston, in his charge, combatted this by saying that it was highly improbable a woman would make such a charge against an entire stranger, without just cause. The jury, however, took the cue. and branded the poor woman as a wretched perjurer, for the sake of the black villain whose guilt was clear as the noonday sun.

At seven o'clock Saturday evening the jury retired for consultation, and remained out all night. Sunday morning there were rumors,—which were evidently sent out from the jury room for the purpose of deceiving the public—that the jury stood ten for conviction and two for acquittal, and that finally one of the latter came over to the majority, leaving but one dissenters. The sequel shows that these reports were false, and that only two of the jury had conscience enough to maintain the guilt of the accused. Four men voted for acquittal on the first ballot while two votes for conviction and the other six by blank votes expressed their doubts in the case. One by one these six came over but the two who held out for conviction, remained true to their consciences until the eighteenth ballot, on Monday evening, when one went over to the side of acquittal, where the six doubtful (?) ones had already ranged themselves. Tuesday morning the long champion of female virtue stood at his post manfully, but after dinner he joined the ranks of the negro worshipers and the farcical verdict was formed.

It was just three o'clock when the came into court, and, with stolid expressionless faces took their seats in the jury-box. There was a brief delay while waiting for the prisoner to be brought in, and then in answer to the usual in terrogatories of the clerk, the forma pronounced the startling words, "NO GUILTY!" A silence like untodeath followed. No one moved, no one spoke. The spectators seemed as though spellbound with horror and surprise. Instinctively th

eyes of all within range sought the faces of the prisoner and his counsel. The negro sat in the box, with a simple smile upon his face, as though scarcely realizing the full extent of his wonderful good fortune. Mr. Higgins sat in the bar, with folded arms and grim visage, his features working with uncontrolled but well concealed emotions. But whatever were his feelings none shared them with him. Not a hand was extended in kindly congratulation, or a word uttered in commendation of his wonderful victory. Among all the people there assembled, he was alone in the hour of his triumph. It was a dearly bought victory.

The prisoner's discharge was ordered, and he went down stairs, accompanied by the two bailiffs. Later in the afternoon, for fear his legally established innocence would not be accepted by the public, he was placed in a close carriage and driven to the State line, above Clay mont, where he was left to follow his own sweet will in the congenial atmosphere of Delaware county, Pa.

As to public opinion in regard to the verdict, it is sufficient to say that it is condemned by ninety nine out of every one hundred people, regardless of party feelings. The jury is execrated on every hand.

FOURTH EDITION.
THE NEAL JURY.
The Verdict of "NOT GUILTY" a General Surprise—Some Talk of Lynching the Released Man.
In a late edition of yesterday's REPUBLICAN, the verdict of the jury in the Neal case was briefly announced. To-day we are enabled to give the following particulars.

Just before the opening of Court yesterday afternoon, a bailiff came down from the jury room, and informed the Judges, who were still in their parlor, that the Neal jury had agreed upon a verdict.

The Court directed that Mr. Higgins be sentior, and that Neal be brought into the dock. After Neal was seated he remained perfectly quiet, his general expression being that of anxiety.

It was some minutes before Mr. Higgins arrived, and while waiting for him the jury were brought in.

The Clerk of the Court, polled the jury and then asked the usual question, "Do you find the prisoner at the bar guilty or not guilty, in manner and form, as he stands indicted?" A breathless silence seemed to settle over the Court room for a moment, which was broken by the voice of the foreman of the jury as he answered in a low tone "NOT GUILTY." Men who had been present during the whole trial, and listened to the chain of evidence that the State had forged around the prisoner could not believe their own ears; and asking the nearest bystander if they had heard aright, turned away thinking that an eminent Pennsylvania Judge was correct, when he said that, "no one but the Almighty knew what the verdict of a pettit jury would be."

Immediately after rendering their verdict the jury left the court room and Neal was commanded to stand up.

The Chief Justice then said: "William Neal, the jury which has tried you have rendered a verdict of not guilty and we now discharge you from custody."

Neal was taken out of the Court room between the two tipstves and conducted to a carriage which was in some mysterious manner already provided and in waiting and rapidly driven away as there were serious threats of lynching him, not only by persons outside but also by many who were in the Court room.

A number of the jurors were approached yesterday afternoon after the rendering of the verdict, but very little information could be obtained. Late last night, however, a representative of the REPUBLICAN succeeded in obtaining the following, which is believed to be correct:

Immediately after retiring on Saturday evening a ballot was taken which resulted in two for conviction, four for acquittal, and six who had not made up their minds.

Four ballots were taken on Saturday night with about the same result, and about half past ten, word was sent down to the Judges who were still in their parlor, that there was no hope of agreeing that night.

On Sunday morning several of the jurymen complained of being sick and Dr. Kirchner was called in to prescribe for them.

During Sunday a number of ballots were taken, and on the eighth and ninth, it was evident that a feeling in the prisoner’s favor was extending, as the last taken showed that there were seven men who were in favor of clearing him, only two for conviction, and three who had no settled opinion upon the matter.

On Monday nine ballots were taken making eighteen in all that had been cast. The last ballot taken on Monday night showed that there was but one man in doubt, while eleven were in favor of acquittal.

There was but three ballots taken yesterday, one in the morning, and one about noon, they both showed the same result as the last ballot cast on Monday night, eleven for acquittal and one in doubt. About half past two yesterday afternoon the twenty-first and last ballot was taken, and resulted in a verdict of acquittal.

Our informant stated that there were several considerations that influenced the jury in their actions, one of which was that they thought the evidence of Mrs. Gosser contradictory in some material points, and it was hinted that if the jury had been instructed that they could have rendered a verdict of assault, or assault with intent to commit a rape, the result might have been different.

THE NEAL VERDICT.—It is a novel
The NEAL VERDICT.—It is a novel mode of defense which the Republican adopts in discussing the false and scandalous verdict rendered by the jury that declared Neal not guilty. That paper resorts to every possible means to rake up excuses for this act of these men, while it declares in plain and emphatic language that it does not agree with the verdict. It says:

"There is no doubt of the fact that the public mind is averse to the verdict, the evidence against Neal being of the most positive character and uncontradicted by the defense. The only doubt in the case was in regard to the resistance, whether it was sufficient, or what might be expected in a case of that kind. Coupled with that was the fact that for many years past only negroes had been executed for criminal offences while white persons equally guilty invariably were cleared."

There is the language of the Republican. It is copied verbatim from its columns. We have not abused the jury nor the Counsel for Neal. The GAZETTE has simply characterized the verdict as scandalous; as of a character that will lead men to believe the men who rendered the verdict did so in violation of the sacred oaths they had taken to render a "true verdict according to the evidence." Could their verdict be true according to the evidence? We leave the Republican to answer, and we quote its own declarations as the best answer. It is printed in italics above, but we will quote it here again. It says the "evidence against Neal being of the most POSITIVE CHARACTER and uncontricted by the defense." And this is assigned as a reason for "the fact that the public mind is averse to the verdict." We should think it was. The public mind has some respect for the wives and daughters of the men of Delaware. Why the decent negroes of the South would not render such a verdict as that. They have more respect for their own wives and daughters than to send forth such a verdict to excuse one of the worst characters that could curse a community with its presence, for committing a crime which all good men detest. Even the savage negro in the wilds of Africa would hesitate but a short while about dispatching a man who had entered his abode and violated the purity of his rude home as Neal did. That he did this the Republican says the proof is of the most positive character and uncontradicted by the defense. What laurels can counsel gain from such a verdict? A verdict rendered upon such a showing could never be worn as an adornment to the cap of a high minded member of the bar—it would never be placed as a rose upon the breast of a just and honest counsellor who held woman in the estimate that she deservedly claims in Delaware. Neal was spirited away to the North, and we leave the jury to their own consciences, hoping that they may never have their happy homes invaded in such a manner as poor Mr. Gosser had. How the Peninsula Papers Comment upon the Neal Verdict.
No act of any Delaware jury ever received such popular condemnation as is showered upon the Neal verdict. Of all the Peninsula papers, but one—the Dover Sentinel excuses it any way. The following editorial extracts will show the drift of public sentiment throughout the state:

Elkton, Md., Democrat:—Delaware soil did not long alter the verdict's rendition support the lusty form of William Neal, for the people who have wives and sisters and daughters, instinctively caught the purport and the probable effects of it. Middletown Transcript:—The verdict is a disgrace to the fair name of the State in which it has been rendered, and the jury that rendered it deserve even more than the wide and general condemnation they are receiving at the hands of the public.

Dover Sentinel:—Unlike the West case, party prejudice and political sentiment seem to be thrown out of the issue in Wilmington, and whether the verdict be proper or unjust we cannot determine, since we neither heard the testimony or were sworn as juror. We do not believe that
Seaford Index:—The verdict of the jury in the Neal case has aroused the indignation of the well thinking people of our State, and caused men to shudder for the safety of their wives, sisters and mothers. It has shaken their faith in the efficiency of the jury system, and in the eyes of many, has clothed Lynch Law with justice and respectability. All this comes of carrying politics into the jury box.

Newark Ledger:—What will be the consequence? When the indignant and suffering people find by sad experience that the tribunals of justice no longer afford any protection, they will take the law in their own hands, and apply a swift and sure remedy. This will be an inevitable consequence, but it is a deplorable alternative which all law abiding citizens must deprecate, for it will sap the foundations of government and tend to destroy the very fabric society.

Georgetown Inquirer:—From the evidence adduced at the second trial as well as that brought out at the first, there seemed but little if any room to doubt that Neal was guilty, and the failure of justice in this case will hardly inspire the people with any very large amount of respect for the twelve men who fathered the verdict.

Dover Delawarean:—Had the crime been committed by a white man the jury which acquitted Neal would, we believe, have found the white man guilty without a dissenting voice. But Neal was a negro and political considerations have prevented the judgment and controlled the action of the jury that tried him. If the example set in this case is to be followed hereafter, there is no protection for the white women of the State, and no restraint upon the vile passions of worthless negroes save such as is secured by the avenging hands of fathers, husbands and brothers.

Middletown Transcript:—Judge Lynch is almost an unknown party in Delaware, and "packed" juries have not been known until now. But with the acquittal of Neal a change has come. A Delaware jury declares by their verdict that the crime of rape upon a white woman by a negro is no crime worthy of punishment. Such a verdict can only have one effect. Public faith will be shaken in the "jury system" and the power of our courts to punish for similar outrages, even where the evidence of guilt is overwhelming. Judge Lynch's court will be opened in Delaware. ANOTHER VICTIM.

LETTER FROM THE MOUNTAINS.
The Pleasure of Summering in the Mountain of the Schuylkill County.
Special Correspondent of the Republican.

TAMAQUA, Pa., July 5th.—Just when or by whom sea side bathing was first introduced, remains a mystery, but we know that to hie away to the mountains was in vogue, away back in the primitive days of the world's history. We read about it in the first books of the Old Testament and it is after all the best way to spend the hot summer months. In the first place it is less costly, and it is less trouble than the sea side watering places. At most of the first class hotels in this region one can obtain substantial board for ten or twelve dollars per week and we do not have to rely on stale vegetables bought in Philadelphia, and carried in the cars away down to the sea shore as they do at Cape May and Atlantic City. Here one may have pure milk and cream, fresh laid eggs, good wholesome butter, and all kinds of vegetables fresh from the gardens. We are enjoying splendid weather just now, just warm enough during the day and the night cool enough to sleep well, while such things as mosquitos are unknown. No one could wish for a better appetite than a bracing walk over the mountain side will give hem if taken in the early morning. The scenery is delightful and it is grand to see old "Sol" rising out of his misty bed beautifully tinting every little cloud and tree.

It is surprising how each succeeding event helps us to forget those that have preceded it. This is brought very forcibly to ones mind, in looking back four or five years, then the "Mollie Maguires," had full sway. No one felt safe and although your correspondent did not live hereabouts then, their whole history is reinvested with interest by hearing the people talk about them, and to read the book that Allan Pinkerton wrote, from notes taken by his detective Jas. McParlan who spent several years with the "Mollies" and became one of their most trusted friends, makes one think truly, "truth is stranger than fiction." Your correspondent visited several places where murders took place. He stood on the spot where in 1876 John P. Jones was murdered by Kerrigan, Doyle and Kelly, as he was going to his daily work. He saw the lamp post where B. F. Yost was climbing up to put out the light when in a minute he was shot dead by McGeehan, a "Mollie." He saw the rum holes where the "Mollies" used to meet which by the way are still run by the widows of some that were hung, and where McParlan, alias Jas. McKenna, used to lay around drunk to all appearances, but awake and sober, as they afterwards found out. Souirr, Que., Sept. 12.—A most disbolical murder was perpetrated last Saturday night at St. Bonaventura, a parish about twenty-seven miles from here, in the District of Ilichellen. It appears that three horse-traders, named respectively Israel Proulx, Joseph Beland, and Antolino Cote, started for St. Hyacinth the Saturday morning, where they spent the day and drank rather freely. SHOT BY HIS SON-IN-LAW.

Louisville, Ky., Sept. 12. Toulght about 6 o'clock, when James Montgomery came to the house of his son-in-law, Sam Duff, to leave Duff's daughter of 8 years, whom Montgomery had given a drive, the two men engaged in an altercation over old family troubles, which had resulted in a separation and divorce between Montgomery and his wife, who now lives with Duff, which resulted in Duff drawing a revolver and shooting at Montgomery five times, four of the balls taking effect. THE TRAIN-ROBBERS.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Sept. 12.—George Banister was arrested today for disturbing public worship at a church in the vicinity of the recent Blue Cut train-robbery. A few minutes before 12 o'clock night before last a most reckless and villainous attempt was made to wreck and rob the Eastbound passenger train on the Central Pacific Railroad at a point about five miles this side of Colfax, Cal. The train was halted by tearing up two rails, thus ditching two engines and one car. The leader of the gang of robbers then called upon Express Messenger Chadwick, who stood in the door of the express car, to hold up his hands and leave the door open. Mr. Chadwick, however, closed and locked the door, then put out the light that was burning in the car, when the robbers at once hastened away, much to the astonishment of everybody, no one having fired a shot at them or in any way molested them.

CRIME.
Ike Stockton, a desperado from New Mexico, was fatally shot at Durango, Col., while resisting arrest.

George W. Hunt, paying teller of the Importers' bank of New York, is charged with the embezzlement of $16,900.

W. F. BRANCH, disbursing agent of the American Transfer company at Bradford, Pa., has been arrested in Toronto for the embezzlement of $150,000.

BURKE & MEYER, wholesale cloth dealers at New York, have caused the arrest of their bookkeeper for the embezzlement of $3,000.

BILL RYAN, the Glendale train robber, was convicted at Independence, Mo., after deliberation for twenty minutes by the jury, and sentenced to imprisonment for twenty years. A motion for a new trial was instantly entered, on the ground of intimidation by Governor Crittenden's presence with armed guards.

The perpetrators of the Arkansas train-robbery have been lodged in jail at Hope, and have been fully identified. One was captured near Sulphur Bluff, Tex., and the other two in the Indian nation. Clark Hull, a conductor on the Iron Mountain road, had the satisfaction of taking one of the robbers.

A PERPERATE attempt was made, at Pallas Green, Ireland, to blow up with dynamite the residence of Captain Thomas Lloyd, occupied by seventeen emergency men and police. Captain Boycott was in Westport recently, and was followed by a mob and burned in effigy. Moffat, the leader of an Orange expedition in County Louth, was fired at and wounded.

MASON, one of the four Central Pacific train-wreckers now undergoing examination at Auburn, Cal., has made a full confession and disclosed the hiding place of tools and arms.

OTTO FREESE, of Aurora, Ill., was murdered on Main street, at midnight, Saturday, by Thomas Oleson, a Swede, 17 years of age. The affair grew out of badinage between two squads. The jail was surrounded by a large and excited crowd all the foremoon, and the prisoner was sent to the county jail at Geneva to avert a lynching.

JOHN AND FRANK McDONALD, of Memononee, Mich., having served two years in the penitentiary, returned for vengeance. They killed William Kittson and fatally stabbed his brother Norman. On the following evening a mob of four hundred battered down the jail door with heavy timber, dragged the prisoners to death on the road, and strung their bodies to trees.

For the purpose of ousting some of the directors a meeting of stockholders of the Nevada and Oregon railroad was called at Reno, Nevada. Treasurer Coffin and two gentlemen from San Francisco were ordered to retire from the room, but did not do so. In a second the air was filled with whistling bullets, fatal wounds being inflicted upon D. W. Balch, of San Francisco, and S. C. Scovill, secretary of the company.

TED FRANKS, the jailer at Bloomington, Ill., was shot through the heart on the 4th inst., by a horse thief named Chas. Pierce. Other prisoners seized the murderer and took the revolver from him. Within ninety minutes a crowd of five thousand persons surrounded the jail, the iron doors were soon forced, and Pierce was dragged out to a locust tree at the corner of Market and Centre streets, and strung up. The shrieks of the villain could be heard above the cheers of the crowd. It was expected that Patsy Devine, the assassin of Aaron Goodfellow, who occupied the cell next to Pierce, would meet the same fate, but he was spared. His being granted a new trial by the supreme court was the inciting cause of the lynching.

Murder at Aurora, Ill.

AURORA, Ill., Oct. 2.—This city has been the scene of another unprovoked murder. Shortly before midnight last night three young Swedes named Thomas Oleson, Ole Oleson, brothers, and Louis Wester, who had been drinking and playing pool in various saloons down town during the evening, started up Main street, near the Congregational church. The Olesons, Wester being on the other side of the street, met a party of young gentlemen who were on their way home from a serenading tour. The latter party had stopped to talk with a couple of friends, whom they had just met, and were singing and making merry among themselves when the Olesons came along. Some good-natured remarks were passed between the Sweedes and the other party about the singing, and Otto Freese, one of the serenaders, laid his hand in a friendly way on the shoulder of Thomas Oleson, when the latter suddenly drew a knife and stabbed Freese in the throat, severing the branches of several arteries, and inflicting a wound from which the young man bled to death before he could be removed from the place where he was struck. Freese, has made all day it that he and his brother obtained the liquor that intoxicated them on the night of the murder from the saloon kept by Daniel Freese, the father of the murdered boy. As both the Olsons are minors, the city authorities can prosecute a suit for unlawfully selling to minors. Active raids have already been commenced against the saloonkeepers for illegal practices, prompted by the recent horrors. Four have been indicted by the grand jury. SHOT DEAD.
LITTLE Rock, Ark., Oct. 10.—Intelligence reached this city today of a terrible tragedy last Saturday at a sawmill near Grand Lake, Ark., a small town on the Mississippi River. William Brooks, proprietor of the sawmill, was beating on employe when a fellow workman named Willian Yountz interfered. Brooks, exasperated, turned upon Yountz, when the latter drew a revolver and fired, the ball striking Brooks in the head and killing him instantly. Yountz was arrested, and after a preliminary examination was discharged.

A DETECTIVE'S FATE.

St. Louis, Mo., Oct. 16.—The body of an unknown man was found yesterday hanging to a tree in thick woods four miles from Grain Valley Station, on the Chicago & Alton Railroad, some twenty miles from Kansas City. The body had apparently been hanging three days. The theory is that the man was a detective, and had been lynched by some one connected with the recent train robbery.

MURDERED FOR HIS MONEY.
Evansville, Ind., Oct. 16.—A colored man named Green was found dead in the suburbs of Henderson this morning, with his head split open with a cooper's adze. A man was arrested on suspicion and lodged in jail. The adze, covered with blood and hair, was found two squares from the body. It is supposed he was murdered for his money.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Oct. 15.—The Iron Mountain Railroad Company yesterday paid Clark Hall and the four men who assisted him in capturing the train-robbers $1,000 each. Moore and Huddlestone have not yet been paid. It is rumored they will sue the company.

EVANSVILLE, Ind., Oct. 16.—Two men giving the names of John Miller and E. C. Brobson were arrested a mile above the city today on a charge of counterfeiting. Spurious coin, molds, metals, etc., were found on them.

S, S. McCall of the corn-canning establishment of Hoopeston, has made an assignment to parties in New York. The cause of his failure is said to be the failure of the sugar-corn crop. He rented 1,500 acres of land near Hoopeston, which he planted in sugar-corn, and for which he paid $4 per acre, and $8 per acre for tending, making a total cost of $12 per acre. The crop was so much of a failure that many acres had nothing at all, and most of it was light. The liabilities of McCall are about $20'000; assets small.

The Lincoln Journal says, "In 1869 a man named Smail was murered on Dalavan prairie. A man named Ott was suspicioned of the crime bnt fled the country and has not been seen or heard of since until his arrest in Leadvill, Col., last week. After killing Smail, he drove forty head of the dead man's cattle to this city and sold them, pocketing the proceeds, and skipped ont for the West.
